newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Americans turn up their noses at French cheese imports.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Americans turn up their noses at French cheese imports.

text.p: The Americans have hit the French where it really hurts. They have committed in Gallic eyes the unpardonable sin. They have criticised French cheese.

From creamy camembert to tangy, blue-veined roquefort, cheese was the subject of Geneva's latest diplomatic battle this week between Washington and the European Union at a United Nations food safety meeting -- which continent's cheese is safe to eat?
The United States angered the EU with its demands for the pasteurisation of dairy products at the meeting of the U.N. Codex Alimentarius Commission, which sets international food safety standards.
To an outsider, the routine -- one might almost say dull -- meeting of negotiators of 150-plus states at a gloomy conference centre dubbed "the bunker" had somewhat surreal overtones.

But blessed were the cheesemakers -- only for now -- after the two sides hammered out a compromise deal in the late hours of Wednesday and decided to defer a vote on the issue to another meeting, negotiators and diplomats said.
"We are here to defend the good name of our cheese," Jean-Pierre Doussin, a member of the French delegation, told Reuters on the sidelines of the meeting.
"Americans say it is impossible to control the cows and milk we make our cheese with. But in France, we make sure our cattle is free from illness and we control the quality of our milk."
If Washington had its way, other countries would be entitled to ban unpasteurised products on health grounds, officials at the Commission said.
The standards set by the joint World Health Organisation and U.N. Food and Agricultural Organisation serve as a reference for the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

In a city more used to negotiating ends to conflicts, smoothing trans-Atlantic ruffles, ironing out global differences and holding disarmament conferences, the cheese talk at the U.N. meeting was heated and sometimes emotional.
"Do we say anything about American hamburgers?," grumbled a European diplomat, referring to European suspicions about the limitations of U.S. cuisine.
Doussin said the principle was at stake. "The issue here is symbolic," he said. "It is a cultural thing."
"For us, Europeans, food is a live element. We respect it, we take care of it. We take pleasure in eating it. Americans eat food to get their protein and calorie needs."
FRENCH PRIDE IN CHEESE

The French pride about cheese -- hard, gooey, crumbly, smelly -- goes back centuries. The French are so spoiled for choice that the late president Charles de Gaulle once observed that a country producing 265 cheeses was ungovernable.
Officials of the U.S. delegation declined to comment.
Under international trade rules, higher standards must be justified scientifically or risk challenge as protectionism.
"The issue here is trade. Human health is not the real agenda," complained a negotiator from one developing country.
French and Swiss cheesemakers were up in arms over the U.S. initiative, attacked in the Swiss media as "American hygienic imperialism".

A Swiss delegate, agriculture ministry official Frederic Brand, said his country was worried about the possible implications on the image of its cheese on the U.S. market, which represented 10 percent of Swiss exports.
"The United States is directly linking lack of hygiene and soft cheese. But not a single person has died in Switzerland from soft cheese because the milk wasn't pasteurised," he fumed.
"We can't understand this American obsession with pasteurisation."
